The scheme, operated through 28 companies and 42 call centers, allegedly lured victims, primarily from Europe, East Asia, and Africa, with promises of high returns. After clients invested money, they were shown fake profits on controlled trading platforms and then blocked from withdrawing funds under various pretexts, such as demanding additional "tax" payments. Investigators estimate the scheme's total transaction volume over two years at 13 billion Turkish lira (approximately $266.4 million), which includes operational expenses. The investigation, involving national intelligence, financial crime units, and Interpol, revealed significant involvement of individuals linked to Israel among the suspected owners and beneficiaries. Authorities have seized assets worth about 1.5 billion lira, along with vehicles and real estate. Real-time news, insights, prices, trending stories, and expert analysis - all in one place.Red Fruit Takes on Four Giants, While iQiyi, Youku, Tencent Video, and MangoTV Fall SilentThe article discusses the rapid rise of the short-video platform Red Fruit (Hongguo), which has achieved a daily active user (DAU) count of 168 million as of July, surpassing the combined DAU of four major long-form video platforms (iQIYI, Tencent Video, Youku, Mango TV) at 155 million. Key factors behind its success include being completely free (contrasting with rising subscription fees on other platforms), successfully attracting older demographics not traditionally served by long-form video, and leveraging its parent company ByteDance's integrated ecosystem (Douyin for traffic, Tomato Novel for IP, and Red Fruit for distribution).

A significant driver is the explosion of AI-generated short dramas, which drastically reduce production time and cost, leading to massive output—over 220,000 new AI short dramas were launched on Douyin in the first half of the year alone. The trend has even extended to celebrities licensing their digital likenesses for AI content.

However, the article notes critical challenges: most short-drama creators operate at a loss despite the platform's potential high revenue, content is becoming oversaturated with low originality, and the "copy-paste" nature of many AI-generated plots and faces poses a risk to diversity. It concludes that long-form video platforms' decline is less about competition from short-form content and more about their own "arrogance"—high costs, repetitive formulas, and complex tiered pricing—failing to meet audience needs for quality and value.
